en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuansou Duan of Mount Jing:
When the ancient patriarchs appeared in the world to benefit others, every glance and every gesture was nothing other than an instruction.

When they presided over great monasteries where many students gathered for study, engaging in debates and verifying the truth of the Dharma, it was impossible for them not to speak. Their disciples and followers would then surreptitiously record these words...
It was preserved and transmitted from generation to generation; its origins reach back to antiquity.

Yet, as the predecessors have passed away and the old regulations have faded into oblivion, those of florid rhetoric have merely gathered together formalities and literary trappings—thus they cannot escape the judgment of the assembly of humans and devas.
For this reason, the discerning have lamented and yearned for the spirit of the ancients. The Elder of Mount Jing, Master Duan, and Yuan’ou, possessed of magnificent virtue...

Renowned throughout the land, he sat in meditation for over twenty years. The fourfold assembly lived in peace and security. Approaching ninety years of age, his hearing remained acute and his vision clear.
He tirelessly propagated the spirit of the school, such that seasoned scholars who had completed their training all turned to him for refuge. He stood towering like a sacred light.
Surveying the four seas, there has been none at this time who could surpass him. The First Seat of the Mountain, Zhengyin, was originally a person of Mongol descent;
having long been close to the practice of *bang* and *he*, his realization was exceptionally profound.
When he passed through my mountain retreat, he brought forth the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of Master Sihui to show me. We sighed together and said: "Dahui late on obtained Fozhao, and after two..."
In a hundred years, we have reached the Master; it has been but three transmissions. Among those of venerable age and noble conduct, we see no others.

Furthermore, since the Southern Song dynasty, Mount Jing has held the most distinguished reputation, having been occupied by Dahui for two periods totaling only seven years, and by Wuzu for eighteen years.
Yet, he treated adversity as favor through the Way, laboring with tireless diligence. What...
"It cannot be avoided; there has not yet been anyone as composed and detached as you, Master. Yin said, "In the past, the words of Zhenjing were prefaced by Lord Su Yingbin;
the words of Ying'an were prefaced by Mr. Qian Songchuang. As for the words of Jingshan, have you not attained the state of 'sentient beings without emotion'?
I replied, "Lord Yingbin had a relationship of mutual correspondence with Zhenjing, and Mr. Songchuang likewise with Ying'an."
I am old and weary; thus, my words may be free from shame. As for this collection, my own ignorance and rusticity are such that how could I hope to equal the two masters?
Nevertheless, regarding Mount Jing, I have gazed up at its precipitous cliffs and sighed that I could not reach them; how then could I dare to compose a preface?
Yet Zhiyin said, "This is precisely what a preface ought to address. Thus, with joy, I shall speak of it: "Prejudiced views and common knowledge are likely..."
It was insufficient to subdue this mountain. Now, the Master’s words are vast and surging like a great ocean; his teaching is expansive and open.
Whether in detailed exposition or concise summary, all are grand and magnificent—like the sound of spring thunder that rouses the insects, or a long wind sweeping over the slopes.
The grasses and trees flourish with joy; yet, reaching these strategic points, they remain hidden and do not manifest, awaiting the right person.

Even in the lingering influence and residual grace of one of great wisdom, there are still such instances. It is like a famous province garrisoned by a veteran general: he maintains a profound gravity, such that even wind and thunder cannot startle him.

Grasping the pivot and executing his commands, he rolls them out or withdraws them according to his own will; this alone is sufficient to ensure that the defensive lines along the square walls remain secure.

There is that which one looks up to and relies upon, from which one dares not deviate; how much more so for a Master who possesses great capacity and great function, who holds the authentic seal of Linji, and who continues the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom? Therefore, I have written this and left it to him.
At this time,
on the thirteenth day of the third month in the first year of the Zhizheng era,
the Preface by the Layman Yong Yují for the Re-engraved Edition of the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuansou Duan from Four Assemblies.

After Master Jizhao (Heshang Yuansou Duan) had entered nirvana, the Duke of Literary Merit Huang of Jinhua composed an inscription for his stupa, and the Grand Master of Literature Yu of Shu County wrote a preface to the records of his four assemblies of discourse.
Both of these gentlemen were renowned throughout the world for their literary excellence, and their works may be considered complete.
Among his disciples who had entered the inner chamber were Qingliang Ziben, Jinshan Huiming, and Tianning...
The Patriarch Chuan again joined his colleagues in requesting, saying: "The records of our late master’s words previously engraved on wood were unfortunately destroyed by war.
Yet, without these, there would be no means to perceive where the Way resides. We fear they might not be transmitted.

Your disciple Bian and two others have already collaborated to commission a carver to re-engrave them. We venture to request that you provide a preface for the opening fascicle. Nevertheless, as for this preface...
It may be abbreviated. Regarding the deeds of my former teacher, many involve supernatural wonders. Those who compose his biography usually avoid recording them;

indeed, followers of the Mahāyāna generally do not delight in hearing of such miraculous matters. However, if they are recorded for the sake of showing them to those entering the Way, it is sufficient to inspire their correct faith.
What harm could there possibly be in this? I wish for these matters to be noted together within the preface; I, Lian, dare not decline.

I, Zi-bian and others, submit this address. Your countenance is fair and your features ancient; your gaze is so piercing it dazzles those who behold it. Beneath your chin, several whiskers stand out stiffly, appearing most majestic.
Like a solitary pine after a snowfall, you stand firm when seated and walk without looking back. Your heroic spirit overwhelms all, remaining as solemn and awe-inspiring as ever.
Wherever you pass, the crowd is already clamoring like thunder; yet upon hearing the sound of your footsteps, they immediately say, "The Secretary Duan is coming."
He remained silent and still as if no one were there. When accompanied by friends and associates, he never spoke of the trivial affairs of the mundane world;

setting aside the Great Dharma, he would not utter a single word. His nature was firm and steadfast, truly unshakable. From the time he became a great monk until his passing, there was not a single night that he slept without his robes on.
When he followed [the master] from Nanping back to Huacheng to receive the scriptures, on a summer evening he opened...

While he was sleeping by the window, a Buddhist monk suddenly arrived, flying with his mendicant’s staff. He engaged him in conversation regarding the essential points of Prajñāpāramitā, speaking incessantly and with great vigor.
After a short while, the monk ascended into the air and departed. When Master Huyan was the abbot of Shuangjing, he once remarked that those belonging to the Daoist school—
There was a previous official who had petitioned the Emperor; his return was very delayed.

When [Master] Gong asked him about it, he replied, "I was selecting the forty-eighth generation abbot of Mount Jing, which is why the celestial gates remained closed for so long. Master Gong’s number exactly matched that count.

When Master Gong traveled to the capital, he dreamed of the Dragon King of the pond at Mount Jing, who held a golden spoon and served him food; the number of times he fed him totaled eighteen. Master Gong...

He presided over the Dharma seat for exactly eighteen years. When the Master was about to manifest his parinirvāṇa, he had the hair and nails he had cut off buried in the Huanyou-an (Monastery of Illusory Existence) at Huacheng.
Upon opening them to view later, śarīras had formed there in profusion. Such among the Master’s remaining deeds as these ought all to be recorded in supplement so that they may be seen by the world;
they must not be omitted. Indeed, the Master’s realization of the Way was in perfect accord with the Buddha’s.
The Patriarch’s fame shook the Middle Kingdom; he was truly one in whom the vital energy of the earth and heavens was concentrated.

The ultimate manifestation of these auspicious responses also arose spontaneously, not comparable to those who dabble in mere supernatural marvels. As Wenxian said: "The prosperity of his lineage was such that its regulations were layered and its patterns repeated;
the Dharma-thunder shook universally, rending the earth and thundering through heaven. And as Wenjing said: "It is like a famous provincial seat, acting as a bulwark..."

As a veteran general, he was profoundly steady and grave; even thunder and lightning could not startle him. Grasping the strategic pivot, he issued commands with complete freedom in their deployment or withdrawal.

This was sufficient to ensure that the garrisons along the Fangcheng Wall had someone to look up to and rely upon, such that they did not dare to overstep their bounds. Were his words not proven true by this trial?
How would I, Leao, dare to add another word? Yet I have reflected that I have heard enough of Wenjing’s learning to understand it in its broad outlines;
furthermore, I have served as his disciple at the gate of Wencian for the longest time. Thus, I have extracted the essence of his discourses and restated them as follows. Alas!
May the Master’s four assemblies of discourse still rely upon my humble writing to be transmitted to posterity. Your son.
Yongtang Bian, Xingyuan Huiming, and Zhongyou Zanchan all established their teachings in specific regions,
and both monastics and laypeople alike looked up to them with reverence.
Preface by Song Lian of Jinhua, Imperial Academician and Attendant Lecturer, Grand Master of the Second Grade with Rank Zhizhao,
Joint Compiler of the National History, and concurrently Assistant to the Crown Prince, on the first day of the tenth month in the winter of the seventh year of Hongwu.

The Discourse Record of the Master at Zifu Chan Temple on Xiangfeng Mountain, Huzhou Prefecture,
compiled by his disciples Falin and others.
On the twenty-eighth day of the eighth month in the fourth year of the Dade era, the Master accepted the invitation at the Laṅkā Hall of Jingshan Monastery.
On the tenth day of the ninth month, he entered the monastery. Pointing to the mountain gate, he said: "The inexhaustible treasury of the gate of spiritual powers;
the inexhaustible treasury of the gate of liberation. Today, right here, it is opened wide with eight characters: the toad leaps up to the Brahma Heaven; the earthworm dashes across the Eastern Sea."
The Buddha Hall: The jade-white brow-hair shines universally throughout the ten directions; the golden hue radiates everywhere across the thousand worlds.
Having paid homage, he takes possession of the room, takes up his staff, and flings open the locks of the golden hall, striking the bell of the jade tower.
One who is not of our own lineage stands tall upon the mountain peaks and wades deep through the ocean floor; such a one is no ordinary monk, but a lion cub.
"Ṭa-sa-di. With a single roar, he stands like a cliff rising ten thousand fathoms high; yet, behind his head, one more blow remains lacking.
Leaning on his staff, he rises. The *Yuan shu* states: "This was bestowed face-to-face by the various officials of the Xuanzheng Yuan; it is called the Vajra Secret Samādhi."
By this, the Māras and heterodox teachers are utterly eliminated, and the True Dharma is made radiant and manifest.
Donor’s Preface: Upon the summit of the solitary peak, where heaven knows not and earth takes no account, for what reason has this one been enticed forth?
For incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the past, he practiced together with the eminent and talented of the entire district to cultivate the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood.

[The Master] pointed to the Dharma seat and said: "This Lion Throne of the Flower Treasury of Universal Radiance—there is not a single person throughout the worlds of the ten directions who does not sit upon it.
To now ascend this high place in such a manner is truly like adding feet to a painted snake."
Holding up the incense: This incense has its roots coiled and its joints interlaced before the time of Vipaśyin Buddha (Viyinwang);
its flames continue and its fragrance link together above the World-Honored One Kāśyapa.

As it is burned in this precious incense burner, it is specifically for the purpose of praying for the longevity of the Great Yuan’s Ruler of the World, the present Emperor—ten thousand years, ten thousand years, ten thousand times ten thousand years! May Your Majesty, reverently, govern ten billion lands of fragrance.
The ocean of water becomes a single ocean of merit, eternal and inexhaustible. The gathering of ten billion Mount Sumerus becomes a single mountain of longevity, towering and immovable.

Next, he offered incense and said: "O Great Wisdom Patriarch, would you rather take this very body to undergo the sufferings of hell on behalf of all sentient beings in the great earth, than ever treat the Buddha-Dharma as mere human sentiment? Thus it was with our late master of Jing Mountain, Zang-sou."
"Upādhyāya, throughout his life he refused to submit to anyone in the four quarters of the world.
Even if Śākyamuni Buddha or Master Bodhidharma were to arrive, he would still have grounds to step back from them.

In years past, while I was in the position of attendant for two years, I exhausted all my ingenuity and employed every skill I had, yet there was truly nowhere for me to find a foothold with him. That is how I came to know him as Dahui."
The rightful grandson. Now, having lit this incense, I offer it to him, and I require everyone’s witness.
He spoke in verse: "If you grasp one pivot, a thousand and ten thousand pivots respond all at once; it is like carving human excrement to make sandalwood incense.

If you raise a single phrase, a thousand and ten thousand phrases flow toward the source; it is like holding a small shell to measure the waters of the great ocean. Is there anyone who is pure and naked? [Is there anyone who is truly bare and unadorned?]

"Refreshing! To be solitary, liberated, and without dependence—come forth and let us verify this together. A monk stepped forward and asked: "The majestic elephant-vehicle descends into the dragon abyss;
the soaring phoenix sits upon a jeweled lotus amidst the mountains. For now, let us set aside the discussion of timing and conditions."
"I wish to hear a single phrase to celebrate the Heaven of Yao. The Master said, "The wind does not whistle through the branches; the rain does not break up clods of earth.
The monk asked, "Master Sansheng said, 'When I meet a person, I come forth; when I come forth, I do not act for the sake of others. Master Xinghua said, 'When I meet a person, I do not come forth;
when I come forth, I act for the sake of others. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "A rooster holding a lamp in its beak."
The monk ran off. A turtle bit his fishing pole. The monk said, "Setting aside for a moment whether you act for yourself or for others, what is the phrase you utter when meeting people?
The Master said, "To know. The monk said, "Setting aside for a moment whether you utter it or not when meeting people, what is the phrase that acts for others?
The Master said, "Urgently. The monk said, "All classes of beings, from devas and humans to the multitudes of living creatures, all receive the power of this grace. The Master— [The text ends here].
[The Master] said, "Those who know gratitude are few. The monk asked, "How was it before you left Shuangjing? The Master said, "Two pieces of skin on the ears.
The monk asked, "How was it after you left Shuangjing? The Master said, "A set of bones for teeth.

The monk said, "When the dragon roars, mist rises; when the tiger shouts, wind is born. The Master said, "Idle talk and long-winded speech. The monk asked, "How was it before you arrived at Fengshan?"
The monk asked, "What is it? The Master said, "A single path where the pines and cypresses grow old. The monk asked, "After reaching Fengshan, what is it like?
The Master said, "The atmosphere of the thousand peaks is majestic. The monk said, "The heavens drape a jeweled canopy and the earth wells up golden lotuses;
everyone knows this. But tell me, what Dharma does the new Fengshan preach today? The Master raised his whisk and said, "I preach this Dharma. The monk [nodded].
[The monk] said: "These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. [The Master] said: "Wrong! The monk said:

"The Provincial Administration Commission, the Provincial Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs, the various officials—both monastic and lay—of this prefecture, the venerable masters of all mountains, and the great patrons have each submitted formal petitions earnestly requesting the Master to honorably preside over this mountain. Furthermore, regarding the single phrase for responding to conditions and benefiting beings—"

"How do you say it? the Master asked. The monk replied, "A single rain nourishes all; the three types of grass and two types of trees. The Master said, "Do not mistake the cry of a crane for the song of a nightingale.

The monk said, "When there is intentionality, one's application is bound to be mistaken; when there is no seeking with intent, all is perfectly as it is. The Master said, "Do not take the cry of a crane and mistakenly call it the song of a nightingale."

The assembly prostrated. The Master then said: "Mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, and forests constantly roar the lion’s roar day and night, universally expounding for devas, humans, and all living beings the unsurpassed, subtle, and wondrous Dharma-gate of liberation.
If one can take up and carry this burden, it has been so for unspeakably, unspeakably many kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, continuing even until the present."
Whether Buddha or Māra, whether sage or ordinary person—each is without distinction, each is clearly manifest.
Should one harbor limited conceptions or fall into the trap of mere views and hearing, one will inevitably merely add further colors to the empty sky.
(He raises his whisk and says: Bodhidharma came from South India to China to transmit this Supreme Vehicle of the One Mind.
This is the Dharma: in heaven, he is as heaven; on earth, he is as earth; among the Sangha, he is as the Sangha; among the laity, he is as the laity.
Regarding the present sagely Son of Heaven, he has manifested through the power of his fundamental and sovereign great vows to successfully succeed to the precious throne of the Golden Wheel.

Throughout ten billion Mount Sumerus and ten billion seas of fragrant water, wherever the sun and moon shine and the wind and rain reach, all receive his majestic spiritual power and submit to his transformative cultivation.
Among the various meritorious nobles of the assembled court, he acts by means of the power of his fundamental sovereign great vows.
Each has established great merit; each has accomplished a vast enterprise. They serve as loyal subjects and filial sons; they excel in both arms and letters.

They are the pillars and limbs of the royal house, and the parents of all living beings. Among the long-standing virtuous elders of this entire prefecture, it is because of their fundamental mastery of the power of great vows.
Illuminating the great potential and manifesting the great function; employing both capture and release, contraction and expansion;

serving as the Vajra Jewel Banner and the True Eye of Maheśvara—for those of pure faith at this Dharma assembly, each shall, by virtue of the roots of goodness planted in former lives, [attain realization].
Though there are ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences, they all do not contradict the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As for the new elder at Fengshan, how will he ultimately act?

(He strikes the whisk. "Above all, avoid boring through tortoises or striking tiles. He further cites: When the Provincial Governor, Attendant Wang, invited Linji to open the hall, Linji ascended the seat and said:
"If we speak according to the school of our ancestors regarding the proclamation of the Great Matter, you have no opening for speech."
"Place! There is no place for you to set foot. On this day, as the Attendant (Changsì) earnestly requested that he reveal the essential principles of the school, a monk stepped forward and asked:
"Whose song does the Master sing? Whom does his lineage of the Dharma follow? Linji said, "When I was at Huangbo’s place, I asked three times and was beaten three times.
As the monk hesitated, Linji gave a shout and struck him again, saying, "One must not seek it in the void."
"In mid-air! The wedge has been driven out! The Master said, "Attendant, you have not forgotten the entrustment;

for the sake of the Dharma, you seek out people. Linji’s great tree stands alone, its shade cooling all under heaven. I dare ask the assembly: Is there a fundamental principle (綱宗) that can be hidden?

Or is there no fundamental principle that can be hidden? If you say there is a fundamental principle that can be hidden, you bury the Elder Master Linji. If you say there is no fundamental principle that can be hidden..."
"Hidden! You have utterly failed your Chief Attendant and your Lord. It is not like this at all. Why was this monk beaten?
[The Master] takes up his staff, draws a line, and says: "A stone ox guards the ancient road; from one horse, three tigers are born."
Small Sermon: All phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds are fundamentally devoid of either reality or unreality. Form has never said, "I am form.
Sound has never said, "I am sound. It is the same for fragrance, flavor, tangibility, mental objects, and the bodies of names, phrases, and sentences—all are thus.
It is simply because throughout immeasurable kalpas you have accumulated dense and heavy evil karma and possess shallow roots of goodness. You have been captivated by forms;
you have been captivated by sounds; you have been captivated by odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects—by names, phrases, and sentences.

Consequently, there are Buddhas whom you admire, sentient beings whom you loathe, paradises for which you yearn, and hells of which you fear. Thus, you remain entangled within the realm of names, phrases, and meanings.
It is like a silkworm making its cocoon; there is no way out.
Tonight, when this mountain monk arrives, if I were to further speak of Buddhas or Dharma, of mind or nature, elaborating on paths and skillfully composing words—what then of Yuquan Pavilion?
What then of Fengshan Pass? This would merely be adding names and phrases upon names and phrases; it would certainly be of no benefit.
The harm [of this] is extremely grave. Time is precious; time does not wait for anyone. Let us all investigate until it is clear and become a monk who is free and unencumbered.
Would that not be a source of lifelong joy? Again, he raised the case: The Second Patriarch asked Bodhidharma, saying:
"May I hear the Dharma-seal of all Buddhas? Mazu replied, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another.

The Patriarch said, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to pacify my mind. Mazu said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will pacify it for you. The Patriarch said, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable.
Mazu said, "I have finished pacifying your mind for you. The Master composed this verse: "To come ten thousand miles is no easy matter."
Matter. What Buddha-dharma is there to be transmitted and upheld? "The mountain hall is still at night; the meditation cushion is cold.
You all should know this for yourselves.
He ascended the hall and said: "Mind is Buddha" is like exchanging honeyed fruit for a bitter gourd. "Neither mind nor Buddha" is like storing precious vessels [in an ordinary jar].
Not impure; not mind; not Buddha; not a thing. Caoxi emerged from Zhengzhou—fortunately, there is no connection here.
Holding up his staff, he said: "This staff has bored its way through Northern Uttarakuru and entered Western Aparagoyānī."
He headed toward Mount Xiangfeng, rising into the clouds and exhaling mist as he departed. *Tap!
Tap!* The fires erupted from the bottom of the great ocean, burning away the Great Image of Jiazhou and the eyebrows beneath its chin. *Tap! Tap!* He descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Bodhidharma is an old, hairy barbarian. Śākyamuni is a dried-up dung-peg. Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are dung-carriers.
The two levels of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment are unenlightened commoners who have broken the precepts. Bodhi and Nirvāṇa are hitching posts for donkeys.

The twelve divisions of the teachings are the registers of ghosts and spirits. The four fruits and three stages of worthiness, as well as the initial mind and the ten stages of the bodhisattva, are ghosts guarding ancient tombs."
"Even if you see it in such a way, you are still mistaking the zero point on the scale.
[The Master] ascended the hall to thank Baozhong Yuan, the Abbot. He cited Master Dazhu, who said:
"I have heard the Master of Jiangxi say that one's own precious treasury is fully complete in all things; its use is sovereign and free, requiring no seeking from without. From this point onward...
At that time, he paused. [The Master continued: "Throughout the entirety of the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single speck of dust that is not one's own treasure.
The Master said: "Master Ma spoke thus for a time; Dazhu heard thus for a time, never forgetting it for the rest of his life."
One thereby attains great enjoyment. Were it not for deep and firm faith, how could one penetrate to the very top and bottom in such a manner?

The Abbot of Zhongyuan once displayed this very Dharma-gate amidst the mountains of Gumo in years past. Is there anyone present who possesses such deep and firm faith as to attain such great enjoyment?
On this day, you have graciously condescended to visit; I hope you will kindly remain with us for a while.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Having shaved your heads and donned the *kāṣāya*, you ought to practice the Holy Path.
All other miscellaneous matters are causes for birth and death. Eating and wearing clothes are miscellaneous matters; gazing at mountains and playing with waters are miscellaneous matters;
even Bodhi, Nirvana, Suchness, and Liberation are miscellaneous matters. Ultimately, what do you call the Holy Path? He struck the whisk.
Son, the young maiden has already departed for the celestial void; the foolish lad still crouches by the fire.

On the occasion of the Lantern Festival, he ascends the hall to express his gratitude to the Supervisor of Receipts, the Master of the Bath, and the Rector. A thousand grains, ten thousand grains—all are born from a single grain.
This single grain—from where does it arise? A thousand lamps, ten thousand lamps—all arise from a single lamp. This single lamp—from where does it arise?
Once you recognize this one lamp, then for a thousand lamps and ten thousand lamps, there will be no doubt regarding lamp after lamp. Once you recognize this single grain...
A thousand grains, ten thousand grains—grain by grain, there is no obstruction. A three-legged donkey trots along, kicking up its hooves and trampling through the boundless seas of fragrant water.
[The Master] picks up his staff and strikes it once: even at the crown of one's head, one must not lack this single blow.
Ascending the hall: This morning is the first day of the third lunar month; the affairs of spring are nearly at an end.
Greens and golds of vegetables and wheat fill the streams, and a gentle breeze sweeps through the four fields. From kalpas past until this very moment, not a single hair’s breadth has ever been lost.
How lamentable are these deluded and ignorant ones, who needlessly chatter and clamor. [Descends from the seat.]
He asked the lay attendant to bring the fire down. "It is not the wind that moves; it is not the banner that moves.
This is the saying of Layman Lu, who sat and cut off people's tongues: it is like a great mass of fire; to approach it is to have one's face scorched."

The Abbot ascends the hall to greet the visiting elders: Amidst green mountains and white clouds, there is nothing to welcome the guest. Herbal medicines are dug up amidst the mist; wild tea is brewed with the dew.
Sitting upon the Panṭa Stone, one lets out a long, solitary cry. [He strikes his whisk and descends from the seat.]
The Imperial Court views the Tripitaka. Upon the conclusion of the ceremony, he ascends the hall:

"Within the *Vairocana-garbha* (the Treasury of Vairocana) there is a great sutra scroll, equal in measure to the trichiliocosm, upon which all matters within the trichiliocosm are inscribed, exhaustively and without remainder.
Now, the Emperor, with his pure celestial eye, beholds this great sutra scroll within a single minute atom (*paramāṇu*). He has earnestly dispatched [this message]..."
The Envoys were granted imperial incense and commanded that all monastic officials throughout the world break open this speck of dust and bring forth this scripture.

They were to cause all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm to know that within every single speck of dust there is such a scripture; within every such scripture, there are such chapters and verses;
within every such chapter and verse, there is such wondrous meaning; and within every such wondrous meaning, there is such [a reality].

How extraordinary! How sublime! How vast! How sovereign! This very morning, following the conclusion of the distribution of offerings, you have again commanded this mountain monk to ascend this seat to proclaim the Unsurpassed Prajñā and to express repentance for the aforementioned merits.
The ocean of wisdom of all various Dharma-gates; the ocean of the marks and characteristics of various causes and effects;
the ocean of various practices, conducts, and vows; the ocean of various skillful means of instruction; the ocean of the ultimate reality of various environments and inhabitants;
the ocean of various mutual interpenetration and inclusion; the ocean of light of various inexpressible-inexpressible merits—all these are universally dedicated.

Turning toward the suchness of the ultimate reality (*tathatā-bhūtakoṭi*), one adorns the unsurpassed *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit. Throughout the four quarters, the anxieties of war and arms are dissolved;

the myriad people delight in the occupations of plowing and sericulture. At such a time, when the eight regions come to court and the ten thousand states present their tribute—how do you express this in a single phrase?
Simply behold the imperial wind forming a single expanse; one knows not where the boundaries of the realm lie.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The mind is not the Buddha; rabbits and horses have horns. Wisdom is not the Way; oxen and sheep have no horns.

Ascending the hall for the Buddha-bathing ceremony: Pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, he claims the foremost rank; having once emerged from the womb, today he appears once more.

This old monk has no other intention than simply to lead you to realize the cause of water.
On a Boat on the Yellow River, Shown to Chan Master Shenzang.
(Two Poems) The first drop can give rise to waves that reach the heavens; Do not follow the current, yet enter the flow. Leap with eyes closed and look with eyes open;
To distinguish clear from turbid, one must look at the source.
The east surges without ceasing, and the west rises again; for your part, do not be surprised by the Yellow River.
These five thousand scrolls of the Vairocana Treasury are already waves rolling incessantly even without a wind.
When the Abbot Ling of Caotang was cremated, his teeth and prayer beads remained unharmed;
they were exceptionally firm and numerous. On this account, he spoke these eight verses:
The fire has cooled and the solitary smoke has subsided; Tranquil, one beholds the original reality. The golden essence is entirely free from dross; The lustrous pearl is utterly devoid of dust.
Not dwelling in the Treasury of Radiance, yet not separated from this defiled body; in a place difficult for celestial Māras to fathom, how many kalpas have passed like the springtime of flowers?
Though the illusory form is understood to be empty, the radiance remains upon the verdant peaks. A single set of teeth against frost and ice; a heart of iron and stone through many lifetimes.
Fierce flames can never consume it; flying dust can hardly invade it. Since the ancient master departed, it has remained desolate until this day.

For thirty-one years, I have cultivated my essence with such diligence that few in the world know of it. Five thousand scrolls of palm-leaf manuscripts and one hundred and eight beads upon my prayer rosary.
Moment after moment there is no distinction; how could mind and mind differ? Like vajras, they are equally indestructible, clearly illuminating the dark thoroughfare.
Today, the cremation is complete; because of you, I laugh and yet I weep. From birth, who was "me"? After death, who will bear my name?
A barren woman conceives at night; a wooden man nurtures a child at dawn. Fundamentally, there is neither form nor characteristic; where, then, could there be loss or peril?
I have already traveled everywhere to visit the ancestral stupas of the East and West. Prajñā is but a manifold body; Nirvāṇa is but a single mind.
The lotus unfolds upon the ocean of awakening; the *campaka* blooms within the grove of dhyāna. After the kalpa-ending fire has raged through all, this pure fragrance rises through past and present.

Having realized the Dharma of the King of Emptiness, one lets heaven and earth come and go as they may. Incidentally dwelling at the Double Path (Shuangjing), one again journeys through the nine lotuses.
The moon is cold upon the golden terrace at night; the wind arises from the jade pool in autumn. My homeland lies upon the River of Chu—whom can I ask for news of my origins?
Birth and death go hand in hand; these matters have always been one and the same. Within the radiance of eternal stillness, amidst the realm of true emptiness.
All sensory objects are without obstruction; all phenomena are entirely interfused. This single bag of skin—when has it ever been "me"?
At the peak of a solitary crag in a ruined house, I recall last year: incense was divided for morning recitations, and we sat side by side at night to practice dhyāna.
The flowers of liberation bloom together; the fruits of Bodhi are shared in their perfection. Why must you depart before me, leaving me alone in sorrow?
Residing in the Mountains (two stanzas):
Mountain trees interlace their branches, and the thatch fills the courtyard. Even the hooves of horses cannot soil the mountain gate. With a lamp lit, I sit facing the snow, composing verses in song.

Verse: Carrying my robe in a fold, I walk around the spring reciting the scriptures; I sleep little, yet always find that tea proves effective. Sickness is frequent, yet I often marvel that medicine lacks efficacy.
The golden garden falls into desolation once every year; Who can compare to the solitary pine, ever green?
A small couch newly set up by the western rock waterfall; white clouds have no path, only the lush grasses. Under the bright moon, the door is bolted as wild monkeys howl;
at the late sun, one wraps oneself in the quilt as mountain birds cry. Generations of poetry and books are but moth-eaten scrolls; ancestral tombs for many reigns are merely plowed fields.
At the inn of Handan, a single meal of millet—how laughable that people of past and present remain so deluded.

Zhongshan is square on all four sides and eight-faceted, utterly inaccessible to climbing. Directly below it is solitary and perilous; its summit pierces through the cold. How many people of this age seek it from the outside?
Yet they rise up peaks and ridges from level ground.
The moon-boat, the ice-wheel, is cold and clear at night; the water and sky are vast and empty. Ten thousand miles of pure radiance are contained within a single oar-stroke.
Seven hundred eminent monks could not lift it up; Huangmei won the right to escort Master Lu.
I present this to the diviner:
my age now stands at eighty-three. The days yet to come cannot match those already past. To inform all quarters, there is no other message:
I have fashioned a cassock from wood to serve as my traveling gear.
I present this to the Daoist physician for his teeth:
a set of clearly defined bones, of which only two or three now remain out of ten.
If you, Master, do not replant them, how will you chew on vegetable roots when you grow old?

Showing Gong the woodcutter that all things share the same root as oneself: whatever the mind turns toward, it is fully perceived. When the opportune moment arrives, a single stroke severs both mind and hand;
a single slice has always been matched by another.
To depict the divine spirit of the layman Huang Dezhong:
within the shadows of empty flowers are the forms of devas and humans; amidst the flash of a flint-stone spark are the shapes of donkeys and horses.
Clearly manifest through kalpas until this very day—how could one ever capture them upon silk with brush and ink?
Having finished writing the preceding verse, Dezhong folded his hands and asked, "At this very moment, is the old man of Jingshan within this, or is he not within this?
The Master said, "The entire great earth is the crown-protrusion (uṣṇīṣa) of you, Venerable Duan;
where would you go to make such a distinction? Dezhong was at a loss for words. [The Master] showed him again:
A single verse has a thousand bodies; Maitreya’s ox bears it upon its horns. Eight-armed Nātha’s horse treads upon its hooves. Within a single characteristic lie all characteristics;
where could Zhang Sengyao distinguish east from west?
The golden scissors reveal a matter from atop the mountain of the five aggregates: all-pervasive blackness and all-pervasive whiteness.
To attain a radiant light that penetrates heaven and earth—listen as the golden scissors proclaim it for you.
The Chan practitioner who has sent Upāsaka Ying to Guangzhou to visit his teacher is no ordinary person.
Every move he makes must transcend the conventional. In every word and every silence lies the treasury of the light of liberation;
in every emergence and every disappearance lies the field for the playful exercise of supernormal powers. Even the thirty-four elders...
Not a companion, he is unwilling to vie with the vast, boundless world. At the crest of the winding valley, at the base of Mount Luofu—there and here, there is neither right nor wrong.
Both Master and Disciple have not yet forgotten; from two thousand li away, they carry their robes and scrolls amidst cold clouds.
When tiger-like sprints and dragon-like gallops meet, wait and watch as a clear breeze rises from the level ground.
The Layman Zhu transformed ginger and taro to provide sustenance for the monastic kitchen.
He then showed him that the ocean of a Buddha’s merit is immeasurable, like space containing all forms;

gardens, clothing, food, and bedding perform all kinds of Buddha-work according to whatever is required. Although ginger and taro are but very humble things, they can eliminate the hunger of the world.
The fire’s heat was unbearable. It took all the lands of the Fragrant Accumulation (*Gandhavyūha*) and caused their fragrances to circulate throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

Thereupon, one knows that all sentient beings possess the boundless merits of a Buddha. The merits of a Buddha are neither existent nor non-existent; the mental capacity of sentient beings is likewise so.
Yet, as for my disciples present here before me, they truly lack both the mind that receives and the object received. *Dānapāramitā*...

Even among the supreme beings of the *pāramitās*, there is neither one who gives nor one to whom it is given; both "existence" and "non-existence," as well as the duality of subject and object, are discarded.
Even the single word "emptiness" is not ultimately real. This is called the most subtle and wondrous state of the Buddha, inconceivable within both the mundane and supramundane realms.
The three lay practitioners Zhao, Li, and Ni established the Lingxiao Assembly and requested a preface for the Shuangjing Monastery located between Wu and Zhe.
Indeed, it is the preeminent peak of the mountains. Tianmu Mountain stands like a screen embracing it from the north, while the Qiantang River winds like a silken ribbon to its east.
Countless layers of peaks and ridges, numbering in the many thousands, are visible only as the exquisite beauty of the Five Peaks.
Lofty and towering, it rivals the azure sky. Below lies the cave of the divine dragon Banaśaka; above, the palaces of Tuṣita and Yāma.
Clear clouds and warm mists rise from the crags and pines; opening at dawn and closing at dusk, they have no end.

Here the Patriarchs took their stand to whip the qilin and lash the phoenix; here spiritual beings relied upon it to provide rain and support the winds. From this, the superior practitioners who investigate the Profundity...
It penetrates the vast array of the universe as a precious seal, clarifying the true principle of the myriad phenomena.

Mounting Sumeru within a mustard seed and rolling the entire dharma-realm upon the tip of a needle—these are all the constant attributes of the fundamental source and original nature; they are neither marvelous functions nor supernormal powers.

All you virtuous people who have ascended this mountain and joined this assembly: your environment is governed by the mind, and phenomena are harmonized with principle. Thus, birth and death are brought to order.

All karmic actions are entirely non-contradictory with the true mark (*dharmatā*). It is as solemn as the Deer Park and Vulture Peak, where a mass of purple-gold light is beheld amidst hundreds of thousands of devas and humans;
the preaching of the Dharma continues to this day without dispersing. Heavenly flowers fall like rain, drifting through the misty void.
Alas! The four modes of birth are in turmoil; white clouds and blue dogs suddenly change and vanish. Driven by the five desires—

Turbulent waves and terrifying surges constantly crash against the boat. Were it not for one whose heart is as pure as ice and whose thoughts are as clear as snow, who could possibly dwell in meditation at this place? Because the Venerable One requested a name from me, I have named him "Pánzhī" (The Staggering). I shall now compose a verse for him. [Verse] The mountain peaks are steep and the cliffs are high; The path is perilous and the precipices deep.

If one does not possess a mind like frost and a spirit like snow, How could one find a way to rest in meditation here? I bestow upon you the name Pánzhī; May you traverse this difficult terrain with ease. Do not let the waves of the world disturb your stillness; Only thus can you realize the Way.
In the past, Master Man’an once resided at Jingyin Monastery; he fully realized the Xianshou school and thoroughly penetrated the meaning of the West’s arrival.
With a single shout, he distinguished the five teachings, and his radiant light illuminated heaven and earth. My son, your name is now Jingyin; by what title do you wish to be known?
My courtesy name is Panzhi; it means "admiring Lin. If you do not obscure these words, how could the ancients be difficult to reach?
Baring my shoulder, I shall shoulder the Great Dharma; let us see if our aspirations will accord.
The Elder Prajñāmātra, using a painting of Vimalakīrti’s inquiry after his illness, requested that a verse be spoken:
"The four great elements are all empty; the five aggregates likewise do not exist. From where does illness arise? From what source does the question originate?"
The one who can be ill and that which is the illness—when they arise, there is nothing that arises. The questioner and the question—when they are raised, there is nothing that is raised.
Since this principle is already thus, all phenomena are entirely without obstruction. In this great gate of liberation, when has there ever been any fetter?
Thirty thousand lion thrones and nine million bodhisattvas entered the chamber of Vimalakīrti, which measured but a single zhang; how could this not demonstrate the indivisibility of space?
The Land of Fragrant Accumulation above is but a mere extension of an elbow’s reach, while the world-system of Abhirati is held within a needle’s point.
Regarding the ultimate destination of all things, how could it ever be apart from this teaching? There is a person of extraordinary measure in this world who dwells in the profound and unfathomable;
through the causes and conditions described above, he performs the work of a Buddha for the sake of the age. Now, with these illusory words, I praise him for but a mere fraction of his greatness.
May all sentient beings universally attain liberation together.
When the Head Seat Qing wiped the sutra, fire-cotton yielded śarīras.

He requested that a verse be spoken regarding this maṇi jewel, which constantly illuminates the world, claiming it emerged from the sutra; yet he was needlessly crude in asserting that it existed because of the cotton.

Deceiving others and deceiving oneself; neither identical nor separate. A brilliance that penetrates the very marrow, chilling and clear; like the rising sun, like the full moon. Unbroken and unmixed, yet manifesting in myriad forms.
One who contemplates in this way is said to practice right contemplation; any other way of contemplating is not so.
This is called "erroneous contemplation.
The moon’s reflection in the pond pavilion is for the sake of the upright and capable Vice Commissioner;
it does not connect with the bright moon flying in the heavens. The clear spring flowing through the earth does not harmonize with that [celestial moon].
Why do the moon and the spring embrace one another? Through the brightness of the moon, all myriad forms are clearly illuminated;
through the purity of the spring, even the finest dust cannot defile it. Because of this purity and brilliance, light and shadow are in perfect harmony.

Illuminating the past and illuminating the present, it shines with crystal clarity through hundreds of thousands of kalpas. How magnificent is Master Gong! The plaque of this pavilion is loftily displayed.

It causes those who ascend this pavilion and lean against the railing to see clearly through their brows and lashes; may the source of the mind always remain thus, forever transcending the karma of darkness.
He had already passed away while seated in his thatched hut. A verse was composed to mourn him:
"The perfectly luminous true nature is beyond cultivation; Throughout kalpas, when has it ever been subject to decay? For fifty-eight years he dwelt in a single thatched hut;
Now, let the fires of karma cremate him as they please."
The six doors of the Tranquil Pavilion are empty, still, and serene, unmoving; let the mundane world be as noisy as it will. Throughout the entire day, no one comes to the steps before me;
only idle clouds accompany my solitude.
The old fisherman has exhausted the waves until not a single bubble remains; for the rest of his life, he is content to grow old in his little boat.
Reclining in the four oceans under a moon as bright as day, he idly takes his fishing cloak as a pillow for his white head.
To Master Shixin:
"The very mind is the Buddha; apart from the mind, there is no other Buddha. To seek externally for a Buddha with form is not your own original, true Buddha.
To Layman Yuanjue: [The same instruction applies.]
The nature of awakening is fundamentally perfect; in every particle of dust, there is no obstruction. The Buddhas and Patriarchs had no other samādhi than this.
In imitation of the poems of Han Shan, forty-one verses:
"The Teacher of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas is none other than this sovereign mind. Vastly encompassing the ten voids, its numinous clarity is wondrous beyond compare."
To cast this aside and seek elsewhere, using clever devices to expound upon principles, is not only to slander the fundamental vehicle (zongcheng), but is also to deceive oneself.
One leaves the household life to study Chan meditation solely for the purpose of resolving the matter of birth and death. When birth and death are not yet resolved, it is no concern of anyone else.
The sick are led away by him; the healthy are put to his service. Though one searches for him, he is not to be found;

he has no name and no title. At the gates of power there is the greedy wolf; he plunders the fat and carves out the flesh. While the individual rejoices within himself, a thousand households weep in sorrow.
Overflowing pits of gold and silver; chests brimming with pearls and jade. Knowing only how to paint the hubs red, one does not realize that one’s own clan is being consumed by fire.
This lump of flesh and blood must also be seen through; food and drink merely sustain it, while clothing briefly wraps it around.

Within this lies the King of Jewel-Awakening, who constantly dwells upon the seat of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). Meeting yet not recognizing one another, we have missed our opportunity for eternal kalpas.
For what reason do you dwell herein? Within this place, all traces of the mundane are severed; at dawn the mists are thick and pervasive, and throughout the night the springs drip and flow.
Jagged mountains on all four sides; a rugged, solitary rock. Reclining high upon it, free from a hundred worries, let spring and winter change as they will.
Within the city is a young man, his countenance like that of an immortal. He wears a garment of fire-washed silk and holds a coral whip in his hand.
He was always mounted on a purple steed; he fell drunk before the spring breeze. For three days we did not see him; it was said he had returned to the Yellow Springs.
My family has a certain thing that comes and goes within the field of the body; I pursue him but he does not leave, I seek him but I do not meet him.
The vastness of the channels is not one of wealth; the vastness of the plunder is not one of poverty. The circular light dazzles the myriad phenomena, like the sun wandering through the void.
Form is fundamentally formless, yet it is divided into that and this; name is fundamentally nameless, yet one attacks what is wrong and affirms what is right.
One morning, with both eyes closed, they are sent off into the desolate mountains. Thistles and weeds pierce their skulls—who cares about them or you?
Yesterday the neighbor to the east died; the neighbor to the west provided funeral offerings. This morning the neighbor to the west died; the neighbor to the east sets out the sacrificial cups.
East and east, then west and west; they circle about, wailing in bitter grief. Unaware of their fundamental true nature, they wander dazedly to the platform of the spring.
Lately, those who dwell beneath the forest trees have mostly become like guests in the dust: they raise wives and rear children, and purchase fields and build houses.
Virtuous fruits do not come in twos or threes, yet evil causes may number in the hundreds or thousands. On another day before King Yama, one fears it will be difficult to evade his retribution.
Throughout antiquity and today, those who study the arts of immortality have refined elixirs and burned cinnabar, hoping to ascend upon purple clouds accompanied by seven dragons and five phoenixes.
In a single morning, these two legs become mere rags; the bones ultimately sink into the mud and sand. The path ahead is as black as lacquer. Alas, O Buddha!
Out of compassion, the Buddha proclaimed golden texts from his golden mouth: three hundred and sixty assemblies and eighty-four thousand gates.
This reveals the nature of primordial existence. According to the faculties of sentient beings, it is like a sword striking empty space; where could one seek its mark?
When humans dwell in this world, each possesses talents suited to their own application. That which is great is not what the small can endure; that which is small is not what the great is fit for.
If Yao were made to lead a sheep and Shun were ordered to whip it, the sheep’s belly would not be filled, while Yao and Shun would merely exhaust themselves in vain.
Amidst their fields, gardens, and thatched huts, men and women gather in circles; they pluck fruit to entertain guests and spin silk to prepare for the state's tribute.
A wife grieves for her husband’s haggard appearance; a mother grieves for her son’s cold body. When one suddenly passes away, she wails and weeps, circling the coffin.
The mind is the source of all phenomena; all phenomena arise because of the mind. When the mind is empty, all phenomena are empty; thus, one escapes the trap of birth and death.
How many people in this world hear the Dharma yet do not listen or accept it? They ride a donkey while searching for another donkey, running about in topsy-turvy confusion and madness.

Some have wives with dazzling complexions; they pluck flowers in the springtime by the waters of Wu. Their embroidered skirts hold golden butterflies; their precious belts are adorned with jade *qilin*.
Mysterious and elegant, she was said to have no rival; graceful and poised, she was deemed peerless. Who would have known that this maiden of the Yang clan would see her bones turn to dust at Mawei?
Leaves fall and the mountain pools grow cold; amidst a thousand peaks, all is profound stillness. One hears only the sound of tigers’ roars; not a single human footprint is to be seen.
Frost and dew moisten the ferns upon the crags; the lunar disc hangs in the azure void. At this moment, contemplating this mind, I sit alone upon the Panṭa rock.
In the world there is a supreme treasure; that treasure is neither blue nor yellow. It exists within the daily activities of men, pure and brilliantly manifest.
The myriad phenomena take him as their master; the myriad dharmas take him as their king. If one does not accord with him, one is like a blind donkey wandering aimlessly.
What are fame and profit? The human heart should not grow despondent. When honor comes, there will inevitably be disgrace; when joy departs, how can there be no sorrow?
Weeds grow anew from the wealthy grave; flowers bloom even at the poor man’s gate. In vain do we toil at plowing and sericulture; our beards turn white and our hair grows thin.
If one knows in life that life is an illusion, then through life one may transcend it. If one knows in death that death is an illusion, then through death one may enter [the Way].
The wise ascend to nirvana; the deluded suffer in bondage. One's own body is Vairocana—simply, one must have sufficient faith.
There are a certain kind of people in this world who possess little substance and much pretense: a piece of brocade upon their lips, yet within their bellies lies a forest of spears and swords.
The true Buddha you do not believe in; you merely mutter the name of Amitābha. Even if you were to see Amitābha, what could he possibly do for you?
This floating world is like a flower in the sky; it must be utterly severed right now. Four snakes dwell together in a single basket; two rats gnaw at the same vine.
The six realms are in constant rotation; the three paths are ever winding and turning. One life leads to hundreds of thousands of lives—when shall there be rest?

From antiquity to the present, it is all a single void; upon whom can one rely to discern fortune or misfortune? A folk song from Ba competes with the "White Snow" aria; earthen jars jostle against the "Yellow Bell" note.

When fortune departs, the tiger becomes a mouse; when the time arrives, the fish becomes a dragon. The wise and brilliant suffer the hardships of poverty, while the foolish and dull enjoy the leisure of wealth.
Reclining amidst a thousand crags, he stands transcendent and apart from the world; he gathers mushrooms for his food and sews oak bark to clothe his body.
Cataracts drench the mossy steps; pool-clouds soak the thatched door. In leisure I chant the verses of the Indian sages, Passing through the slanting rays of the sun time and again.
Human life does not last a hundred years, Yet karmic burdens are of a thousand kinds. Deceit and guile fill the bowels, Greed and avarice saturate the lungs and liver.
Deceived by sounds and deluded by forms, one is cheated by the realm of color; yet to escape the cycle of saṃsāra—how truly difficult this is!
High and cold within the mountains, few people come to ascend them; the pines sway with a tinkling of snow, while creeping vines entwine in a dense veil of mist.
The mountain flowers do not bloom in spring; the lake ice does not melt until summer. What is there to do while dwelling here? The source of the mind is profound and still.
I dwell upon the mountain peak where white clouds never part. The windows and doors are covered with ivy; the paths to the gate are layered with moss.
The mountain fruit has been stolen by a monkey; the cliff flower is offered by a deer. For many years there has been nothing to do; I sit in a heap upon the rocks. Paper is not thin for being thin;
it is only when people are thin that they are truly thin. A tiger is not evil for being evil; it is only when people are evil that they are truly evil.
The ferocity of a tiger may still be warded off; the wickedness of man is difficult to grasp. Thin paper may still be handled; a fickle person is hard to rely upon.
Heaven is cultivated by oneself; hell is not created by another. Why not return early to take refuge in the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment?
In the Eastern Sea, the dust of the *páng* plant swirls; the green mountains have become level plains. The peach blossoms of Queen Mother Wang lie far away, their location unknown.
How much time does human life possess? Yet we stubbornly harbor anxieties for a thousand years. A *bājiāo* plant wishing to endure winter will wither prematurely as autumn arrives.
Polishing a brick will not produce a mirror; digging the earth makes it difficult to find heaven. Why sit here in bitter exhaustion? You must learn the Tathāgata-dhyāna.

If you wish to recognize the Tathāgata-dhyāna, it is ever manifest throughout kalpas: when rolled up, it resides within the square inch of the heart; when unfurled, it pervades the great trichiliocosm.
Jīvaka could not obtain the wondrous; the fierce fire opened the golden lotus.
I report this to you, seekers of the profound mystery: you must awaken with urgency. Both "mind" and "Buddha" are but empty names; this floating life lasts but a fleeting moment.
Do not wait for impermanence to arrive. It is like applying medicine to a goiter only when one is about to marry.

I laugh at a certain kind of person who, throughout their life, has been prone to negligence; they have never mastered the study of the scriptures, yet as soon as they open their mouths, they revile the Buddha.
"Buddha" means "awakened. Why must you revile him so bitterly? The ancient Buddhas departed long ago; your insults are merely for their sake.
Awakening is simply awakening to one's own mind, constantly keeping it free from defilement. Like a precious moon within lapis lazuli, its radiance penetrates both past and present.
Outside the mind there is no separate Buddha; outside the Buddha there is no separate mind. If you do not believe in this mind, you will drift and sink for long ages within the six realms.
This is the teaching of the Great Sage of the West, and even the words of Confucius; we have not transmitted it erroneously—you must listen to it!
The Patriarch’s Iron Ox Mechanism: empty space has no locks. A boat rocks upon Mount Sumeru; fire burns within the great ocean. To let it go does not belong to another;
to bring it back, how could "I" exist? Alas! You mute sheep-like monks—like tigers watching a water mill.
High atop the lofty peak, all is silent and no one wanders there. Smoke and clouds rise day and night; the trees on the cliffs rustle in the wind.
Cranes nesting nearby serve as neighbors, and wild deer are my companions. When thirsty, I drink from the water at the base of the crags; when cold, I wear a coarse cloth robe.
Grappling at the vines, I ascend the perilous peaks; treading upon stones, I peer into distant recesses. I linger, leaning against a pine tree to sit; looking down and up, I rest from time to time.
Encountering spring, it is just like winter; in summer, it is always like autumn. Having lived long years without fetters, what cause for sorrow could there be for the rest of one's life?
Those sons of the marketplace in the east and west burn their skulls with the fire of suffering. Failing to bring this present life to an end, they further bind themselves in enmity for future lives.
What matters is there in this life? In daily conduct, simply keep the mind level and even.
Though pearls, gold, and silver may fill one's house to the rafters, in the end, none can avoid the journey to the Northern Mounds.
The root causes of the illnesses harbored by sentient beings differ; thus, the Buddhas speak of medicinal flavors as distinct. These distinctions are not real, and these differences are illusory.
When illusion is exhausted and reality reaches its ultimate limit, the fundamental state is simply suchness (*tathatā*).
Cause and effect are as clear as looking at one’s own palm; do not pass your youth in vain with superficiality. This skin-sack exits only to re-enter it again;
the vast expanse of the six realms of existence brings nothing but sorrow to the heart.
In the heavens, the sun sets and the moon rises; upon the mountains, leaves fall and flowers bloom again.
In the Yellow Springs, one sees only those who depart, but never a single person who returns.
One should cultivate oneself early while it is still timely; when will joy and pleasure ever come to an end?
Those children in Chang’an, draped in sable furs and brocade, fear only that there are no ropes to bind the white sun.
The karmic winds beat upon the withered skull; the greedy mind is like the ocean, never knowing contentment. The Buddhas realize this and ascend to Nirvana;
sentient beings follow from this path into hell.
When phenomena pass away, they are all empty; when phenomena arise, they fundamentally do not exist. I beg you to listen to my words: do not drink the wine of ignorance.
Praise of Avalokiteśvara (two stanzas):
With thirty-two manifested bodies and fourteen powers of fearlessness, like the sun traveling through the void, where can any trace be found?
The scaled dragons in the basket are alive and leaping; to pick them up is already to fall into the second rank.
On the subject of the Arhat paintings:
all truths are empty, non-existent in the world to come. Their supernormal powers shift through a hundred transformations, beyond all models or names. One knows not where their traces may be found.
Traces. Yet they have been passed down by others as painted scrolls.
Who can caption this "Diagram of Tending Cattle"?
Whose desolate pasture stretches across the plains? Where does a solitary village nestle among tall trees? The official fields have been plowed out; the oxen are at work.
At leisure, one plays the horizontal flute against the eastern wind.
Venerable Subhūti praised the rain of flowers, which once moved Kauśika; his layered praises are rare in this world. A pity that such a thing lies as a coarse thorn in one's hand.
Li. At that time, he did not strike him across the back or pull him by the collar.
Venerable Piṇḍola praised his wondrous supernatural powers and gave him every indulgence; however, I shall ask him clearly: when he raised his hand to brush his eyebrows, was it ever [not so]?
Let it go. How can one say that when afflictions have not yet been emptied, Hanshan and Shide were praised with verses and poems?
Since they were merely rustic and rural folk, I do not believe them to be Mañjuśrī.

The number of disciples he ordained is such-and-such, and those who succeeded his Dharma and simultaneously propagated his teachings throughout the regions of Wu, Chu, Min, Yue, Shu, and Han are such-and-such in number.

The Master’s deeds and conduct shall be recorded by me, Puṃ, upon this stele. I, Puṃ, am but a descendant of those who wear the ceremonial cap and the wide-sleeved robes;
I have not yet been able, within the lineage of the Buddha’s school, to inhale the fragrance of the *campaka* flower or taste the essence of the *amṛta*.

Thus, I know not how to compose words to praise him. Nevertheless, I have set forth in full what is described in his formal biography, providing a preface and composing an inscription for it, so that [his legacy] may not be lost.
In truth, it is simply that those who come to study are thereby able to exhaustively investigate the ultimate purport. The inscription says:
The Great Hero proclaimed his extinction, and the paths of the school first diverged. Had there not been the single transmission, who would have enlightened us?
Lofty was the Great Wisdom, casting its shade over four generations; the prosperity of its gate and courtyard followed one pattern after another, like overlapping squares and circles.
The Dharma-thunder shook far and wide, splitting the earth and roaring through heaven. Seated upon the Lion Throne, he served three successive reigns for forty-two years;
imperial favors and extraordinary honors were bestowed upon him in abundance, and both sovereign and ministers followed his lead like the wind.
A formidable external protector and a main pillar of the Great Dharma, he collapsed in a single night. Yet, being fundamentally without birth or extinction, how could there be going or coming?
Quiescent yet ever-illuminating, like the autumn moon in a azure pool; Radiating as a thousand rays of light, neither identical nor distinct.
Mount Jing is vast and verdant, its peaks reaching the clouds; The True Body abides eternally—on what does Great Wisdom rely?
To praise and describe empty space would be either folly or delusion; I have recorded this directly according to the original text, And carved it upon this mountain stone.
*The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuansou Duan, "The Sun Shining Universally" (Huiben Zhengbian Furi Puzhao), Volume Eight (End)* Postscript to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuansou Duan:
All phenomena have no inherent essence; that which is taught is nothing but mind. Failing to perceive one's own mind, one gives rise to conceptual discrimination.
Now, observing the recorded teachings from the four assemblies of Chan Master Yuansou of Mount Jing, each one flows forth from within his own breast.
As for their wondrous function, it is like marshaling a million heroic soldiers at a distant frontier; none can withstand their vanguard.
As for their skillful means, it is like gathering a hundred rare and strange objects in a thoroughfare; those who arrive may explore and take whatever they find. In their gathering and releasing...
"Transverse and longitudinal, he has attained great mastery. Dàhuì said:
"It is like taking a famous variety of Fuzhou lychee, peeling it, removing the pit, and placing it in your mouth; it is simply that you cannot swallow it yourself.

By this, one knows that the Chan Master has received the orthodox transmission of the five leaves of Great Wisdom (*Mahāprajñā*) and is able to magnify his ancestral lineage. As for those who have not yet obtained the fish or the rabbit...

One should not forget the fish-trap once the fish has been caught. On the first day of the New Year in the Guiwei year of the Zhizheng era, Miaodao respectfully inscribed this beneath the eaves of Zhushan;
he was eighty-seven years of age at the time.
